stem: What is the $y$-coordinate of the $y$-intercept of the graph of $y = f(x)$ in the $xy$-plane?
stimulus: The graph shows part of the linear function $f$, which a printmaker fitted to measurements from a series of etched plates.

figure.caption: Printmaking: linear function f
figure.alt: A line segment falling from left to right through the points (2, 14), (4, 11), (6, 8) and (8, 5). The segment is drawn only from x = 2 to x = 8.

explanation: The line is not drawn as far as the y-axis, so you have to extend it yourself. Pick two points on the line, such as (2, 14) and (4, 11). The slope is (11 − 14)/(4 − 2) = −3/2. The y-intercept is where x = 0, which is 2 units to the left of (2, 14). Moving 2 units left on a line with slope −3/2 raises y by 3, so the line crosses the y-axis at 14 + 3 = 17.

common_errors.why: Gave the y-value at the left end of the drawn segment (x = 2) and did not extend the line to x = 0.
Used a slope of +3/2 instead of −3/2, so moving left from (2, 14) lowered y by 3 to get 11.
Inverted the slope to −2/3 (run over rise), so moving 2 units left added 4/3 to 14.
Found the x-intercept (where y = 0, at x = 34/3) when the question asked for the y-intercept.

stem: The graph of $y = f(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis at the point $(a, 0)$. What is the value of $a$?
stimulus: The graph shows part of the linear function $f$, which an immunology lab used to model results from its assays.

figure.caption: Immunology: linear function f
figure.alt: A line segment falling from left to right through the points (0, 8), (3, 6), (6, 4) and (9, 2). The segment is drawn only from x = 0 to x = 9.

explanation: You need the x-intercept, which is where y = 0, and the drawn segment stops before it gets there. The line starts at (0, 8). From (0, 8) to (3, 6), y drops 2 for every 3 units to the right, so the slope is −2/3. To fall the full 8 units to the x-axis, the line needs 8 ÷ (2/3) = 12 units to the right. So a = 12.

common_errors.why: Gave the y-intercept, where the line crosses the y-axis, instead of the x-intercept.
Took the right end of the drawn segment as the x-intercept, but y = 2 there, not 0.
Inverted the slope to 3/2 (run over rise) and got 8 ÷ (3/2) = 16/3.

stem: In the $xy$-plane, the graph of $y = mx + b$, where $m$ and $b$ are constants, is shown. What is the value of $b - m$?
stimulus: A marine biologist uses the line shown to summarize a set of reef survey readings.

figure.caption: Marine biology: the graph of y = mx + b
figure.alt: A line falling from left to right through the points (−1, 8), (0, 5), (1, 2), (2, −1) and (3, −4).

explanation: Read the two values separately. The line crosses the y-axis at (0, 5), so b = 5. Step 1 unit right from (0, 5) to (1, 2), and y falls by 3, so m = −3. That makes b − m = 5 − (−3) = 8.

common_errors.why: Took the slope as +3 even though the line falls from left to right, so got 5 − 3 = 2.
Inverted the slope to −1/3 (run over rise) and got 5 − (−1/3) = 16/3.

stem: What is the $x$-coordinate of the $x$-intercept of the graph of $y = f(x)$ in the $xy$-plane?
stimulus: The graph shows part of the linear function $f$, which a textile historian used to model measurements taken from archived woven samples.

figure.caption: Textile history: linear function f
figure.alt: A line segment rising from left to right through the points (−8, −9), (−4, −6) and (0, −3). The segment is drawn only from x = −8 to x = 0.

explanation: The x-intercept is where y = 0. The drawn segment ends at (0, −3), which is the y-intercept, so you have to extend the line. From (−4, −6) to (0, −3), y rises 3 for every 4 units to the right, so the slope is 3/4. To rise from −3 to 0, y has to go up by 3, which takes 3 ÷ (3/4) = 4 units to the right. The line crosses the x-axis at x = 4.

common_errors.why: Gave the y-intercept, where the drawn segment ends on the y-axis, instead of the x-intercept.
Moved in the wrong direction from (0, −3). A rising line reaches y = 0 to the right of the y-axis, not the left.
Inverted the slope to 4/3 (run over rise) and got 3 ÷ (4/3) = 9/4.
